item.title: 13 ghost employees, 134 salary stoppages uncovered in Education Ministry payroll check
item.description: 13 officers have been identified as ghost employees within the Ministry of Education, while the salaries of 134 other officers were stopped after a payroll verification exercise uncovered outstanding permanent appointment documentation. Education Minister Aseri Radrodro says the 13 ghost employees were identified following a verification exercise conducted in response to recommendations from the A
item.content:encoded:
13 officers have been identified as ghost employees within the Ministry of Education, while the salaries of 134 other officers were stopped after a payroll verification exercise uncovered outstanding permanent appointment documentation.

Education Minister Aseri Radrodro says the 13 ghost employees were identified following a verification exercise conducted in response to recommendations from the Auditor-General’s 2024 report.

The report raised concerns about officers who were no longer employed by the Ministry but continued to receive salaries during the 2024 financial year.

Radrodro says the verification of salary payments is an established process and is not a new exercise.

He says it is part of the Ministry’s responsibility to ensure employment records are accurate and public funds are paid only to legitimate employees.

Meanwhile, the 134 officers were affected by the cessation of salary payments in Pay 18/2026 after outstanding permanent appointment documentation was identified during the verification exercise.

The Minister says the affected teachers had already been issued permanent appointment contracts, but their signed contracts were not returned to the Ministry on time for processing and updating of their employment records.

As a result, the relevant information was not reflected in the Fiji Education Management Information System, or FEMIS.

He says the issue was identified during subsequent payroll verification.

The Ministry says the payroll verification exercise is aimed at ensuring the accuracy of its employment records and that salary payments are made only to officers who meet the required employment and documentation requirements.

item.title: High carbohydrates, low protein intake found among older Fijians - Hawea
item.description: Research conducted among older Fijians in the Central Division has found that protein intake remains a major nutritional concern, with many older adults consuming relatively high amounts of carbohydrates and fats but not enough protein. The research was conducted in collaboration with the University of New South Wales and FNU.
item.content:encoded:
Research conducted among older Fijians in the Central Division has found that protein intake remains a major nutritional concern, with many older adults consuming relatively high amounts of carbohydrates and fats but not enough protein.

The research was conducted in collaboration with the University of New South Wales and FNU.

Speaking during an oral presentation at the Pacific Islands Health Research Symposium at Fiji National University in Nasinu, FNU Lecturer in Nutrition and Dietetics Salanieta Hawea says the findings highlight the need for older people to include more protein-rich foods in their daily diets to support healthy ageing.

She says adequate protein is particularly important as people age, as it helps maintain muscle mass, muscle strength, physical function and overall wellbeing.

Hawea says older adults need sufficient protein to maintain their physical capacity and strength as they grow older.

She says a diet lacking adequate protein can make it more difficult for older people to maintain muscle mass and physical function.

Hawea stresses that older people should be encouraged to consume more protein-rich foods rather than relying heavily on carbohydrate-based meals.

Haw ea says the wider health challenges facing Fiji’s older population also highlight the importance of better nutrition.

She says the study found that some older people also had chronic diseases, including diabetes and other long-term health conditions.

Hawea says greater emphasis is needed on ensuring older people consume adequate protein and other essential nutrients to support healthier ageing.

item.title: You don’t need to be wealthy to invest in shares - SPX CEO
item.description: Ordinary Fijians can become shareholders in companies they know and support without needing to be wealthy or financial experts. This is according to South Pacific Stock Exchange Chief Executive Officer Sheraj Obeyesekere, who says there is a misconception that the stock market is only for sophisticated or wealthy investors.
item.content:encoded:
Ordinary Fijians can become shareholders in companies they know and support without needing to be wealthy or financial experts.

This is according to South Pacific Stock Exchange Chief Executive Officer Sheraj Obeyesekere, who says there is a misconception that the stock market is only for sophisticated or wealthy investors.

Obeyesekere says the South Pacific Stock Exchange is licensed by the Reserve Bank of Fiji to facilitate the buying and selling of shares in companies listed in Fiji.

He says the main function of the stock exchange is to connect companies that need capital for growth with everyday Fijians and institutions that have funds they would like to invest.

He says SPX currently has 21 companies across multiple industries that have listed their shares for trading, with investors buying and selling shares in those companies daily.

Obeyesekere says people can start small and do not need a large amount of money to begin investing.

He says people can own a small number of shares and become shareholders in companies they already know and support.

He says SPX already has investors from villages and outer islands, showing that investing in shares is not restricted to people living in major centres.

Obeyesekere says it is encouraging to see successful businesses interested in listing their shares on the stock market, as this creates opportunities for everyday Fijians to benefit from their growth.

He says when listed companies are successful and profitable, shareholders can benefit through dividends, where they receive a portion of the profits, or through an increase in the value of their shares.

He says giving everyday Fijians the opportunity to own shares and benefit from the growth of successful businesses is inclusive and commendable.

He describes this as “democratising corporate growth”, where everyone is given an opportunity to benefit from corporate growth.

INSERT: SPX CEO on shareholders 4th Sept

Obeyesekere says stockbrokers can assist investors with the technical side of investing, including ratios and other analysis.

He says there are also qualitative signs people can consider when assessing whether a company is performing well.

He says extensive advertising, strong profits and being a strong player in the industry can be positive signs, although people should understand an investment before putting their money into it.

However, Obeyesekere stresses that investing in shares comes with risks and share prices do not always rise.

He says investors should consider the performance of individual companies as well as wider economic events that can affect share prices.

The CEO says diversification is one way investors can manage risk by spreading their investments across different industries.

He says Fijians should also continue using other savings and investment avenues such as FNPF, unit trusts and the banking system.

He says investing in shares should be considered as one part of a diversified approach to saving and investing.

item.title: Rescue of two workers raises hope for more than 150 trapped in Nepal tunnels
item.description: Fresh hope has emerged in Nepal for more than 150 workers believed to be trapped in hydropower tunnels in the Trishuli Valley following the rescue of two workers after nine days underground. One of the survivors, S anjay Sah, says he chanted mantras to help him endure the ordeal and remained in contact with three of the four other people trapped with him.
item.content:encoded:
Fresh hope has emerged in Nepal for more than 150 workers believed to be trapped in hydropower tunnels in the Trishuli Valley following the rescue of two workers after nine days underground.

One of the survivors, S anjay Sah, says he chanted mantras to help him endure the ordeal and remained in contact with three of the four other people trapped with him.

The second survivor, Kabir Maharhan, has been taken to hospital and is in a critical condition.

Around the same time, rescuers retrieved a body from the tunnel. Authorities believe the person may have died in floodwaters while attempting to escape.

The workers have been trapped underground since Wednesday, 26 August, when a glacier collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border triggered catastrophic flash flooding.

More than 1,300 people have been confirmed dead, while more than 5,300 remain missing following the disaster.

At least 39 workers are believed to remain trapped in the Trishuli 3A tunnel, while more than 100 others are thought to be trapped in similar tunnels across the valley.

An expert has told the BBC there could be a potential "Goldilocks zone" inside the Trishuli 3A tunnel, where conditions may be suitable for survival.

Rescue teams continue to face extremely challenging conditions as they work to reach those still trapped underground.

Nepal's Energy Minister says the rescue efforts will continue, stressing that hope remains as long as there is a possibility of finding survivors.

item.title: No one charged yet in alleged overseas employment scam involving more than 300 Fijians
item.description: Crystal Robanakadavu · 04/09/2026 Police had earlier confirmed to fijivillage News that a report has been lodged at the Namaka Police Station and an investigation is underway.
item.content:encoded:
Crystal Robanakadavu · 04/09/2026

Police had earlier confirmed to fijivillage News that a report has been lodged at the Namaka Police Station and an investigation is underway.

More than 300 people claim they paid $100 each after being promised overseas employment opportunities, with some expecting to travel to Australia.

They say over 50 people reportedly turned up at the Nadi International Airport last Saturday expecting to travel overseas but later discovered that there were no flight bookings for them.

Some of those affected had reportedly resigned from their jobs in preparation for the promised overseas employment.

The Ministry of Employment is urging those affected to lodge reports with Police and stresses that workers are not required to pay recruitment fees to participate in Government-facilitated overseas employment programmes.

item.title: Doctors urge Fijians not to wait for heart attack symptoms to worsen
item.description: Fijians are being urged not to wait until chest pain becomes unbearable before seeking medical attention, with cardiologists warning that delayed treatment can lead to more serious heart damage and complications. As Fiji observes World Heart Month under the 2026 theme, "Don't Miss a Beat", Interventional cardiologist Dr Srikar Miryala says many patients seek specialist care only after their condit
item.content:encoded:
Fijians are being urged not to wait until chest pain becomes unbearable before seeking medical attention, with cardiologists warning that delayed treatment can lead to more serious heart damage and complications.

As Fiji observes World Heart Month under the 2026 theme, "Don't Miss a Beat", Interventional cardiologist Dr Srikar Miryala says many patients seek specialist care only after their condition has significantly deteriorated or they have already suffered a heart attack.

He says recognising symptoms early and seeking immediate medical attention can improve treatment options and outcomes.

Dr Miryala says early intervention can sometimes allow patients to undergo less invasive procedures such as angioplasty or stenting.

Since March last year, he has been performing primary, or emergency, percutaneous coronary intervention procedures at PSH Hospitals.

The procedure is used to restore blood flow during a serious heart attack caused by the complete blockage of a major coronary artery, helping to minimise damage to the heart.

Dr Miryala also says substance abuse and high consumption of kava and fizzy drinks are among the other concerns contributing to heart disease in Fiji.

Award-winning cardiothoracic and vascular surgeon Dr Sanjeev Kumar Khulbey echoed the same sentiments saying that lifestyle choices are also contributing to Fijians developing heart-related conditions at younger ages.

With 30 years of experience as a cardiac specialist, Dr Khulbey says people, particularly those over 40, need to take greater responsibility for monitoring their health.

He says Fiji has access to fresh fish, fruits and vegetables, yet many people continue to rely on canned and processed foods.

According to Dr Khulbey, heart disease can be linked to lifestyle choices, existing medical conditions and genetics, although many risk factors can be reduced through healthier eating, regular exercise, avoiding tobacco and limiting alcohol consumption.

He says every household should also have a blood pressure monitor and blood sugar monitor to help people regularly keep track of their health.

Dr Khulbey is also warning people against relying on herbal medicines or homemade remedies when they are unwell, urging them to seek professional medical advice instead.
